sentences.text: Strigogyps was approximately the size of a large chicken or guan, weighing less than one kilogram.
The type species Strigogyps dubius was described by Gaillard in 1908.
This species is based on a single tibiotarsus found in the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene Quercy phosphorites of France.
The original tibiotarsus of S. dubius was destroyed during the bombing of Munich in World War II, though casts remain.
Lambrecht described Eocathartes robustus and Geiseloceros robustus in 1935 from the Middle Eocene Geisel Valley of Germany.
Mayr (2007) determined that Eocathartes robustus and Geiseloceros robustus are synonymous and represent the species Strigogyps robustus.
The species Strigogyps sapea was likely flightless based on the ratio of its wing to leg bone lengths.
Strigogyps had legs not adapted for running, suggesting a walking lifestyle similar to that of trumpeters.
While other Cariamiformes were mostly carnivorous, Strigogyps sapea likely had a facultatively herbivorous or omnivorous diet.
Strigogyps belongs to the order Cariamiformes, but the Paleobiology Database lists it within the family Strigidae.
Recent studies suggest Strigogyps is a basal member of Cariamae and not closely related to phorusrhachids.
Salmila robusta is considered more basal than Strigogyps, with the clade of Salmila and Cariamae being the sister taxon to Psophiidae within Gruiformes.
Strigogyps fossils date from the Middle Eocene to the Early Oligocene periods.
Strigogyps lived in France and Germany during the Middle Eocene and Early Oligocene.
Strigogyps lived between 48.07 and 33.9 million years ago, from the Lutetian to the Priabonian stages.
It is debated whether fragmentary remains from the Palaeocene and Eocene of England and North America are phorusrhachids, though they are likely not.
